poet.name: Mir Anis
poet.tagline: The foremost Urdu marsiya poet of Lucknow, remembered above all for his elegies on the tragedy of Karbala.
poet.module_status_note: Phase 1 (Identity) + Phase 2 (Bibliographic Foundation) + Phase 2B (Primary Edition Resolution) + Phase 2C (Rekhta Reader & Primary-Text Accessibility) done. Rekhta's actual digitized reader was opened directly this phase and found genuinely paywalled (no page content accessible) with only a genre-level table of contents. No edition tested so far (5 scans + 1 gated reader) has yielded verifiable primary text. All 10 verses remain at Strong Secondary (B) — 0 upgraded to A, 0 downgraded. 'Kulliyat-e-Anis' still does not match any real edition found. Phase 3 (large-scale primary-text extraction) has NOT started. See research_notes and Mir_Anis_Module_Research.md for the full Phase 2C findings, including two independently-caught AI misattribution examples that inform this module's source-corroboration rules.

father.value: Mir Khaliq (also written Mir Mustahsan Khaliq)
father.note: A marsiya poet in his own right; source_status B.

family_background.value: Born into a multi-generation family of poets. Several sources describe the family as writing Persian and later Urdu poetry across multiple generations.

grandfather_lineage.note: Sources disagree on Mir Anis's exact relation to Mir Hasan (author of the celebrated masnavi Sehr-ul-Bayan). One set of sources describes Anis as Mir Hasan's grandson; a source consulted for this module instead named the grandfather as 'Zahak' and Mir Hasan as great-grandfather. Not resolved — do not treat either version as settled without checking a primary genealogical/critical source.

date_of_birth.note: Wikipedia gives 1800 (citing one source for 1803 CE); other secondary sources (Rekhta) give 1803. Recorded as an open conflict per the research plan's rule not to silently pick one.

date_of_death.day_conflict: Sources disagree on the exact day: 1 December 1874 vs 10 December 1874.

education.value: Early education in Faizabad; studied Arabic and Persian. Reported to have been well acquainted with Hindi literature (Tulsidas, Malik Muhammad Jayasi). Reportedly composing couplets by age 4–5.
education.note: Early-childhood composing-ability claims are common in poet hagiography generally and should be treated cautiously pending a primary/academic source.

teachers.value: Reported to have studied under the poet Shaikh Imam Bakhsh Nasikh.

literary_output_scale.value: One secondary source (Rekhta) states approximately 200 marsiyas (elegies), 125 salams, and 600 rubais. A separate, more concrete figure now exists for the original Naval Kishore print run specifically: 108 elegies, 268 quatrains and 31 salaams across its 4 volumes (1876–77) — see collection col-naval-kishore-1876. The two figures are not the same claim (one is an approximate lifetime-output estimate, the other a specific print run's contents) and should not be conflated.
literary_output_scale.source_status: C for the ~200/125/600 estimate; B for the Naval Kishore print-run count

connection_with_lucknow.value: Based in Lucknow for most of his literary career, reciting majlis (mourning assemblies) there and, after the 1856 British annexation of Awadh, reportedly travelling to recite in other cities as well.

contemporary_poets.value: Mirza Dabeer — a contemporary marsiya poet regarded as Anis's great rival; secondary sources describe separate literary 'schools' (Anisia and Dabiria) forming around the two.

patrons.value: Secondary sources associate his rise to fame with the reigns of Nawabs Ghazi-ud-Din Haider, Amjad Ali Shah and Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh — not yet confirmed against a primary/academic source.

burial_place.note: Not established from sources consulted so far.

family_members_who_were_poets.value: Father Mir Khaliq; brother Mir Munis Lakhnawi (per one secondary source); sons reported as Mir Salees and Nafees Lucknowi; grandsons reported as Arif Lakhnavi and Rasheed Lakhnavi.
family_members_who_were_poets.note: Family-tree claims from a single secondary source; not cross-checked.

historical_context.summary: Mir Anis worked in Lucknow (Awadh) during a period — late Mughal decline, then Awadh under its own Nawabs until British annexation in 1856 — often described as a high point of Urdu literary culture, court patronage, and Shia religious/cultural life. Marsiya as a genre was already established before Anis (with earlier Lucknow and Delhi marsiya poets), and is closely tied to the recitation (majlis) culture of Muharram.
historical_context.caveat: This is a general-consensus summary from secondary sources, not a researched historical account. It should be expanded and cited properly in a later research pass (Phase 1/7 of the plan) before being treated as authoritative.

literary_context.anis_position: Widely described in secondary/tertiary sources as having brought the Urdu marsiya to its highest literary form, comparable to his great-grandfather/grandfather Mir Hasan's status in masnavi.
literary_context.caveat: This is a broad characterization repeated across popular sources; needs grounding in specific academic literary criticism (Section 21 of the plan) rather than being stated as fact.
literary_context.editorial_history_note: A named, sourced fact now exists that partially substantiates the 'foremost marsiya poet' characterization from a different angle: Dawn's literary-notes column (source src-dawn-parekh-2023) describes roughly 50 years / three generations of dedicated scholarly effort (Masood Hasan Rizvi Adeeb, continued by Nayyar Masud and Timsal Masud) to establish an authoritative text of Anis's elegies — a level of editorial attention the column implicitly treats as unusual, which is suggestive of his stature but is not itself a literary-critical assessment. See critical_reception.

genres.description: Elegiac poetry mourning the martyrdom of Imam Hussain and his companions at Karbala; Anis's primary and best-documented genre.
genres.source_status: A/B mixed — well documented that this was his primary genre; individual poem counts unverified

genres.description: Shorter elegiac/salutation poems, also Karbala-related, recited in majlis.
Quatrains; the Naval Kishore print run alone contained 268 (see col-naval-kishore-1876) — a real, sourced print-run figure, though still not the same thing as a verified total lifetime output.
genres.source_status: B for the print-run count; C for any claim about total lifetime output

genres.description: Secondary sources note Anis wrote comparatively little ghazal, with marsiya being his dominant form.
Mentioned in the research plan's genre list; not yet confirmed for Anis specifically in sources consulted.
genres.note: Do not assume attestation — flagged for the next research pass.

collections.name: Kulliyat-e-Anis
collections.note: Referenced generically in popular sources as 'the complete works of Anis.' This module has not yet independently confirmed which published edition(s) use this exact title, who edited them, or whether a genuinely complete Kulliyat exists versus a large-but-partial compilation. Per the research plan (Section 10), 'Diwan-e-Anis' and 'Kulliyat-e-Anis' must not be assumed interchangeable — still not resolved. The concrete, real editions found this phase (col-naval-kishore-1876, col-fazil-lakhnawi-1974, col-aaj-ki-kitaben-111) are NOT titled 'Kulliyat-e-Anis' — none of them use that exact name — so this entry remains a separate, unconfirmed lead rather than being merged with any of them. PHASE 2B UPDATE: targeted catalog searches (HathiTrust catalog, WorldCat, Google Books) for "Kulliyat-e-Anis" / "Kulliyat Anis" / "کلیات انیس" found no matching library record. Combined with the finding that none of the five real editions now identified (Naval Kishore 1876-77, Fazil Lakhnawi 1974, Saleha Abid Husain 1980, Aaj Ki Kitaben 111-marsiye, the 2004 reprint) carry this exact title, this module's working conclusion is that "Kulliyat-e-Anis" is most likely an informal/generic descriptor people use online for "the collected marsiyas of Anis" in general, rather than the name of one specific real publication — but this is a conclusion from absence of evidence in the sources checked, not a confirmed negative, so the entry is kept (status unchanged) rather than deleted.

collections.status: confirmed to exist as digitized volumes
collections.note: Rekhta hosts these as separate digitized volumes under two slightly different title patterns ('Marasi-e-Meer Anees' and 'Marsiya Haye Meer Anis Sahab Marhoom'). Whether these are the same underlying compilation, different editions, or different compilations entirely has not been determined. NEW this phase: a plausibly related but not confirmed-identical item was found directly on Archive.org (col-archive-2004-reprint, publisher 'Munshi Nawal Kishore Press, Lucknow', dated 2004) — same publisher lineage/name as the original 1876 Naval Kishore print run, but a 2004 date, so almost certainly a modern reprint rather than the original 1876 print. Not merged with this entry — flagged as a related, unreconciled lead.

collections.name: Naval Kishore Press original edition
collections.status: historically documented, not directly examined by this module
collections.contents: Volume 1: 28 elegies, 29 quatrains, 3 salaams. Full 4-volume set: 108 elegies, 268 quatrains, 31 salaams.
collections.source: Dawn.com 'Literary notes' column by Rauf Parekh (5 June 2023)
collections.note: This is the first-ever print collection of Anis's marsiyas, per this source, and the origin of the '108 elegies' figure that later scholarly editions (see col-aaj-ki-kitaben-111) treat as their base text. No editor is named for this original print run in the source consulted. No direct scan of the original 1876–77 printing has been located by this module — do not confuse with col-archive-2004-reprint, a different, later dated item under the same press name.

collections.name: Muntakhab Marasi Anees
collections.editor: Syed Murtaza Hussain Fazil Lakhnawi (سید مرتضی حسین فاضلؔ لکھنوی)
collections.publication_year: October 1974 (a later reprint by the same publisher is referenced elsewhere as c. 2000, not independently confirmed by this module)
collections.status: confirmed — corroborated by two independent sources (a literary-history newspaper column and the Archive.org catalog record for the actual scanned book)
collections.contents: A scholarly selection of 12 elegies, chosen and annotated with reference to handwritten manuscripts and multiple editions, per the Dawn source.
collections.note: The most scholarly-credentialed source identified so far for verse-level verification — manuscript-referenced and annotated, per its own description. An OCR text file exists for this scan (Archive.org's *_djvu.txt derivative) and was attempted in this pass, but OCR quality was too degraded for reliable verbatim quotation (see research_notes) — it was NOT used to source any verse in this dataset. Re-attempting extraction from this specific edition (via the PDF/page-image derivatives rather than raw OCR text, ideally with human proofreading) is the single highest-value next step for reaching A-level verses.

collections.name: Anis: 111 Marsiye
collections.editor: Nayyar Masud and Timsal Masud, building on research by Masood Hasan Rizvi Adeeb
collections.publication_year: 2023 (per one secondary source) — NOT independently confirmed; may reflect the year the Dawn column discussed it rather than a confirmed publication date
collections.status: described by the source as the current 'authentic version'
collections.contents: 111 elegies: the 108 from the original Naval Kishore print run plus 3 more drawn from rare Tej Kumar Press editions. Represents roughly 50 years / three editorial generations of work, per the source, and explicitly grapples with the fact that Anis himself revised couplets and added stanzas across different manuscript versions of his own work.
collections.source: Dawn.com 'Literary notes' column by Rauf Parekh (5 June 2023)
collections.note: Publication year is the weakest-confirmed field here (single source, possibly conflated with the article's own date) — treat as unverified until a publisher/library record is checked. No open digital scan has been located (and, being a 2020s commercial Karachi publication, likely still in copyright, so none should be sought outside legitimate channels). This is nonetheless the most important single bibliographic lead from this phase: it is the only source that directly documents Anis's own textual revisions across manuscripts, which is exactly what plan Section 22 (textual variants) anticipates.

critical_reception.assessment: General secondary/tertiary sources consistently describe Anis as the pre-eminent Urdu marsiya poet and note a historic rivalry/comparison with Mirza Dabeer (the 'Anisia' and 'Dabiria' schools). No specific named academic critic's assessment has been sourced yet for this module.
critical_reception.note: Placeholder — Section 21 of the research plan requires named critics with dated, sourced assessments. None collected yet.

critical_reception.critic: Masood Hasan Rizvi Adeeb (with later editorial work continued by Nayyar Masud and Timsal Masud)
critical_reception.source: Reported in Rauf Parekh, 'Literary notes: Mir Anees's 111 elegies in three volumes: authentic version', Dawn, 5 June 2023
critical_reception.date: Editorial work spanning roughly 50 years / three editorial generations, per the source; culminating edition dated 2023 per the same source (unconfirmed independently — see col-aaj-ki-kitaben-111)
critical_reception.assessment: Not a literary-critical judgment of Anis's poetry as such, but a documented, sustained scholarly effort to establish an authoritative text of his elegies from manuscript variants — itself indirect evidence of the seriousness with which Anis's corpus is treated by specialists. Earlier editors (Ali Hyder Nazm Tabatabai, Masood Hasan Rizvi Adeeb's own predecessors, Muhazzab Lakhnavi) are described by the same source as having produced editions 'lacking in references and other important details.'
critical_reception.interpretation: This module treats this as evidence of scholarly consensus on the DIFFICULTY and IMPORTANCE of establishing an authentic Anis text, not as a quoted critical opinion of the poetry's merit.
critical_reception.note: This is the first named-critic/named-source entry in this dataset that isn't a placeholder. Still short of what plan Section 21 wants (a specific critic's assessment of the poetry itself, ideally with a direct quotation).

research_notes: PHASE 2 (Bibliographic Foundation) done this pass, on top of the existing Phase 1 (Identity) seed. Phases 3, 6, 8–10 (page-level verse verification, full non-Karbala poetry, marsiya structure mapping, complete critical reception, Anis-vs-Dabeer, final full QC) remain NOT done.

Real, named editions now identified: the original Naval Kishore Press print run (1876-77, 4 vols — col-naval-kishore-1876), Syed Murtaza Hussain Fazil Lakhnawi's scholarly 1974 selection (col-fazil-lakhnawi-1974, scan available), and the Aaj Ki Kitaben 111-elegy edition edited by Nayyar Masud & Timsal Masud building on Masood Hasan Rizvi Adeeb's research (col-aaj-ki-kitaben-111, year unconfirmed). None of these is titled 'Kulliyat-e-Anis' — that generic collection entry (col-kulliyat-anis-generic) remains an unresolved, separate lead.

The Marsiya → Edition → Volume → Page → Original Text path (the objective of Section 5 of this phase's instructions) is NOT yet established for any individual marsiya in this dataset. We know editions exist (with real editors/publishers/years) and we know marsiya text exists (via Rekhta/Wikisource), but we have not yet mapped which specific marsiya sits in which specific volume/page of which specific edition. Every collection_id field on individual works/marsiyas/verses is null for exactly this reason — left blank rather than guessed, per the plan's anti-hallucination rules.

An OCR-based verse-extraction attempt against the Fazil Lakhnawi 1974 scan's *_djvu.txt file was made and explicitly abandoned: the OCR text was too degraded for confident verbatim quotation, and the extraction was mediated by an AI summarization step that itself introduces error risk on top of OCR error. No verse in this dataset was sourced from that attempt. Re-attempting this — ideally via the page-image/PDF derivatives with human proofreading, not raw OCR text — is the highest-value next step toward actual A-level (primary verified) verses.

Verse corpus grew from 1 to 10 couplets, all via a consistent method: locate a couplet on Rekhta's index or Wikisource, then attempt independent corroboration via a second source (a search-result snippet or an independent AI-generated summary quoting the same lines). 7 of the 10 (0001, 0002, 0003, 0005, 0006, 0007, 0010) have two- or three-source corroboration; 3 (0004, 0011, 0012) are single-sourced from Wikisource only. All remain at Strong Secondary (B) — none have been checked by this module against an actual primary edition page, so none qualify as A per the module's own rules, regardless of how many secondary sources agree. Note: two Wikisource fetches were mislabeled by the fetch tool as containing more couplets than they actually delivered ('5 couplets' and '4 couplets' headers over text that was actually only 3 couplets/6 lines each) — this dataset only recorded the couplets actually present in the returned text, not the mislabeled counts, which is why verse_ids skip from 0007 to 0010 (0008/0009/0013 were never populated because no corresponding text was ever received).

One textual variant was encountered and recorded (anis-verse-0007-var-a): a one-word difference ('گھڑے' vs 'کھڑے') between the Rekhta-index-adjacent phrasing and the Wikisource transcription. Per plan Section 22, this was NOT silently resolved — both readings are recorded, with the Wikisource reading kept as the displayed text for a stated, non-evidentiary reason (it was the more directly fetched source), not because it was confirmed more accurate.

anis-marsiya-003 / anis-verse-0010–0012 is an important cautionary case, documented in-line in the dataset: the popular association of 'Jab ran mein sar-buland Ali ka alam hua' with Hazrat Abbas is NOT supported by the couplet text itself (which only says 'Ali ka alam', never naming Abbas), and an AI web-fetch tool used during this research pass asserted the Abbas identification as if it were textually explicit — a live example of exactly the kind of unverified inference the plan's anti-hallucination rules exist to prevent. The character field was deliberately left empty on these verses and the Hazrat Abbas character entry was NOT updated to link them.

The Aaj Ki Kitaben 111-elegy edition's 2023 publication year is single-sourced and may simply reflect when the Dawn column was written, not a confirmed publication date — flagged as unconfirmed rather than stated as fact.

The Dawn source is the first evidence in this dataset of Mir Anis revising his own verses across manuscript versions ('alter[ing] couplets or add[ing] stanzas') — directly relevant to plan Section 22 (textual variants) as a methodological warning, even though no concrete instance of Anis's OWN cross-manuscript revision (as opposed to a transcription-level difference like anis-verse-0007-var-a) has been located and documented yet.

Two of five Wikisource marsiya-page fetches were declined by the fetch tool on (mistaken, in this module's assessment) copyright-caution grounds, since Wikisource specifically hosts this material because the 19th-century originals are public domain. This is a tooling limitation encountered during research, not a finding about Wikisource's reliability as a source — noted here so a future pass doesn't waste time assuming the block reflects an actual rights issue.

Carried over from Phase 1, still unresolved: birth year (1800 vs 1803), death day (1 vs 10 December 1874), and grandfather/lineage (Mir Hasan as grandfather vs great-grandfather, with a 'Zahak' claim for the grandfather generation).

No page numbers, specific editions, or specific editors have been confirmed for any individual verse or marsiya (as opposed to the collections themselves, several of which now have real editor/publisher/year data). Every such field on verse/work/marsiya records is intentionally blank rather than guessed.

PHASE 2B (Primary Edition Resolution) done this pass. Goal was resolution, not expansion: 0 new verses were added (well under the 10-verse cap), 3 new editions/collections/sources were added (col-saleha-abid-husain-1980 plus its source_registry/edition_registry entries), and a new edition_registry[] (6 entries) and edition_page_map[] (7 entries, all 'unresolved') were added.

Directly tested OCR quality on 2 scans this phase (Fazil Lakhnawi 1974, Saleha Abid Husain 1980) via targeted phrase search for this dataset's 3 best-attested matlas — both scans' OCR was assessed unreliable/garbled, and none of the 3 phrases could be confirmed found in either. This is inconclusive (not proof the marsiyas are absent from these books), but it does mean neither scan is currently usable as a primary text source via this module's tooling (WebFetch has no image/vision capability, so page images could not be inspected directly).

Kulliyat-e-Anis investigated further: targeted searches of HathiTrust's catalog, WorldCat, and Google Books found no record under this title. Working conclusion (not a proof): 'Kulliyat-e-Anis' is most likely an informal, generic descriptor rather than the name of one specific real publication. The col-kulliyat-anis-generic entry's source_status/bibliographic_confidence was downgraded to E to reflect this.

Attribution audit performed on all 7 marsiyas (marsiyas[].attribution_status): 3 confirmed_by_text (Hurr, Aaj Shabir/Imam Hussain, Farzand-e-Payambar/Imam Hussain), 1 uncertain (the Abbas association on anis-marsiya-003, unchanged from Phase 2), 3 unassigned (no character claimed, nothing to audit).

Bibliographic confidence and text/verse verification are now explicitly tracked as separate dimensions per plan instruction: edition_registry[].bibliographic_confidence (how sure we are the edition exists/is correctly identified) vs. verses[].source_status / verification.level (how sure we are the exact wording is genuine). An edition can have bibliographic_confidence B while contributing zero verified verse text, which is exactly the current state for every scanned edition in this dataset.

All 10 existing verses were re-checked against the 2 newly OCR-tested scans and left unchanged at B — no upgrade to A (no primary match confirmed), no downgrade (no contradicting evidence found either). Each verse's verification object now carries checked_against_primary:false and a primary_check_notes field documenting this attempt, so a future pass can see what was already tried rather than repeating it blindly.

Remaining blocker for Phase 3: this module has no way to read page IMAGES (only OCR text, which has proven unreliable on every scan tested so far) — until either a higher-quality OCR pass, a vision-capable tool, or human proofreading is available, no marsiya can be reliably linked to a specific edition/volume/page, and no verse can be upgraded past B. This is the single concrete blocker referenced in the final answer below.

PHASE 2C (Rekhta Reader & Primary-Text Accessibility) done this pass. 0 new verses added (limit was 5). 2 new source_registry entries, 0 new collections/editions (ed-rekhta-digitized and ed-saleha-abid-husain-1980 were updated in place with new fields, not duplicated).

Rekhta's actual e-book reader (not just its index/search pages) was opened directly for the first time this phase: it is a real 438-page flip-book with genuine metadata (Tej Kumar / Dr. Aditya Behl contributors — cross-referencing the Dawn article's 'Tej Kumar Press' mention independently), but actual page content is paywalled ('exhausted 5 free content pages per year') and the visible table of contents is genre-level only (مرثیہ/رباعیات/سلام section headings with page numbers, no individual poem titles) — so even with access, this specific index would not by itself confirm which marsiyas the volume contains.

ghazalsara.org was checked as a 4th independent site confirming anis-verse-0001's matla wording — but like Rekhta's marsiya-index pages, it cites no book/edition/page. More agreeing sources does not equal a primary check; verification level intentionally unchanged.

CAUGHT MISATTRIBUTION (new example, same failure class as the Phase 2 Abbas case): a WebSearch summarization tool, asked about anis-verse-0002/0003's marsiya ('آج شبیر پہ کیا عالم تنہائی ہے'), stated it 'is a ghazal by Mir Taqqi Mir' and appears in 'Mir's Kulliyat' — this is WRONG. This exact text is Mir ANIS's marsiya, already independently confirmed via Rekhta, Wikisource, and an earlier search-snippet corroboration in Phase 1/2. Mir Taqi Mir is a different, earlier (18th-century) poet. Nothing in this dataset was changed because of this false claim — it is recorded here specifically as a second, independent demonstration of why this module never accepts a single AI-generated summary as evidence, and always requires corroboration from an actual source page.

Archive.org's own archive-hocr-tools metadata for the Saleha Abid Husain 1980 scan reports 96% OCR 'confidence' and does provide a scan-page-to-printed-page mapping structure (_page_numbers.json) — but this module's own direct reading of the same file's OCR text found it heavily garbled, and a targeted phrase search against it found none of 3 known matlas. This contradiction is recorded, not resolved — the 96% figure is a character-recognition metric, not a semantic-readability guarantee, and should not be read as evidence the scan is currently usable.

Result: 0 of 7 marsiyas achieved a complete citation chain (marsiya → edition → volume → page → visible original text). 0 verses upgraded to A. 0 verses downgraded. 0 textual variants confirmed (ghazalsara's text was not compared word-for-word — only its matla was independently checked against the dataset and found consistent). The Abbas attribution question remains uncertain — no new evidence was found this phase (Rekhta's marsiya-index page for that specific poem was already checked in Phase 2 with no citation found, and this phase's new leads — the ebook reader and ghazalsara — don't reach that specific poem's text either).
